paragraphs: Advertising attribution assigns credit to platforms involved in an advertising outcome. The paper studies how to assign that credit when platforms supply reports that may affect their own attribution. It formalizes the problem using mechanism design, bringing incentives into an evaluation often based on rules such as giving all credit to the latest report.

The authors show that, within their model, this last-click rule does not make truthful reporting a dominant strategy and performs poorly on accuracy and fairness. They propose the Peer-Validated Mechanism, where each platform’s attribution depends exclusively on other platforms’ reports. They prove that this mechanism is dominant strategy incentive compatible: truthful reporting is a best strategy regardless of what other platforms report.

The analysis provides accuracy bounds for both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings. The stronger optimality result applies specifically to the homogeneous setting, where the mechanism is optimal among incentive-compatible alternatives of the stated kind. Numerical experiments also find better accuracy and fairness than last-click attribution. Together, these results connect attribution quality with the incentives created by the credit-allocation rule.
neurips-2025-beyond-last-click-an-optima.tldr: A peer-validated attribution mechanism encourages truthful reporting and is provably optimal among DSIC mechanisms in the paper’s homogeneous setting.

paragraphs: Boltzmann Generators sample physical configurations by transforming a simple starting distribution into a more useful one. Recovering the desired physical statistics requires reweighting samples using their likelihoods. Computing those likelihoods through a continuous normalizing flow involves expensive Jacobian calculations, creating a bottleneck for larger molecular systems even when generating samples is practical.

BoltzNCE learns an energy-based model that approximates these likelihoods. Its training combines noise contrastive estimation with score matching, and the authors find that using both objectives works better than either alone. In two-dimensional synthetic systems, noise contrastive estimation improves the relative weighting of different modes compared with score matching alone.

For alanine dipeptide, the resulting energy distributions and free-energy profiles closely resemble those produced using exact likelihoods, with 100-fold faster inference. Training across multiple dipeptides also supports transfer to new systems; with some fine-tuning, the method achieves at least a sixfold speedup over standard molecular dynamics. The contribution focuses on accelerating likelihood evaluation so that reweighting remains practical, with the reported physical agreement demonstrated on the studied systems.
neurips-2025-boltznce-learning-likelihoo.tldr: BoltzNCE learns approximate likelihoods that accelerate molecular sample reweighting while closely reproducing exact-likelihood results on the studied systems.

paragraphs: Visual instruction tuning teaches multimodal models to connect images with language-based requests, but processing large training collections is expensive. Selecting a smaller collection can help, provided it contains useful examples and enough variety. CoIDO addresses the difficulty of balancing those two goals, which earlier approaches often treat separately while also spending heavily on dataset evaluation.

The method trains a lightweight scorer on a small random portion of the candidate data. It jointly learns importance and diversity through an uncertainty-based formulation that balances the two objectives. Once trained, the scorer evaluates the full candidate collection, allowing examples to be ranked and selected directly without an additional specialized selection algorithm.

In the reported experiments, scorer training used 20% of the data, and the final instruction-tuning subset also contained 20%. Across ten tasks with LLaVA-1.5-7B, this subset retained an average of 98.2% of full-data fine-tuning performance. CoIDO also had the lowest training FLOPs and highest aggregate accuracy among the compared competitors, supporting joint scoring as an efficient selection strategy in this evaluation.
neurips-2025-coido-efficient-data-select.tldr: CoIDO jointly scores importance and diversity to select a 20% training subset that retains 98.2% of full-data performance in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: ContextAgent studies how an assistant can recognize when help would be useful from the circumstances surrounding a person. Existing proactive approaches described in the paper either inspect restricted environments such as desktop interfaces or issue notifications through fixed rules. The proposed system expands the available context to sensory information from wearables, including video and audio.

Its workflow separates understanding the situation from deciding whether to act. First, it extracts multiple kinds of context from sensory observations to infer user intentions. It then combines that context with personas derived from historical data to predict whether proactive service is needed. When assistance is warranted, it automatically invokes the tools needed to provide it.

The authors introduce ContextAgentBench to evaluate this task, with 1,000 samples spanning nine everyday scenarios and twenty tools. On this benchmark, ContextAgent achieves accuracy improvements of up to 8.5% for proactive predictions and 6.0% for tool calling over baselines. These results support the usefulness of surrounding sensory context for both recognizing opportunities to help and selecting the actions that deliver that help.
neurips-2025-contextagent-context-aware-.tldr: ContextAgent combines wearable sensory context and historical personas to predict when assistance is needed and automatically call appropriate tools.

paragraphs: Competitive programming provides demanding tests of coding and reasoning, but duplicate or closely related problems can distort evaluation. CPRet approaches this issue through retrieval: finding relevant code or related problem statements in a collection. Its dataset combines automatically collected problems and solutions with manually curated annotations, and separates training and test data in time.

The benchmark contains four retrieval tasks. Two connect text and code or compare code with code. The other two search for duplicate problems and connect simplified descriptions with their full versions. The authors train separate retrievers for these needs: CPRetriever-Code uses a Group-InfoNCE objective to align problems with code, while CPRetriever-Prob specializes in similarity between problems.

Both retrievers achieve strong reported results and are released for local use. The paper also examines LiveCodeBench and finds that highly similar problems raise model pass rates while making models harder to distinguish by performance. This finding gives retrieval a role beyond helping locate solutions: it can support evaluation that explicitly accounts for problem similarity when interpreting apparent coding ability.
neurips-2025-cpret-a-dataset-benchmark-a.tldr: CPRet introduces competitive-programming retrieval data and models, and shows how similar problems can inflate pass rates and weaken benchmark differentiation.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce answers that contradict visible or factual evidence. The paper targets this problem while trying to preserve general reasoning performance. It identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches: preference optimization can shift output likelihoods in ways that harm broader capabilities, while contrastive decoding based on manually degraded images may poorly represent genuine hallucinations.

Decoupling Contrastive Decoding learns separately from positive and negative examples in preference data. It trains distinct positive and negative image projections inside the model instead of optimizing the examples as pairs. The negative projection learns patterns associated with actual hallucinations and supplies vision-aware negative images for contrastive decoding during inference.

This design connects learned hallucination patterns with an inference procedure that suppresses their influence. Avoiding pairwise optimization alleviates the likelihood-displacement issue, and learned negative projections remove the need for handcrafted image degradation. Across the reported hallucination benchmarks, reasoning tasks, and ablations, DCD matches direct preference optimization’s hallucination suppression while preserving general capabilities. It also outperforms the evaluated contrastive methods that use handcrafted perturbations.
neurips-2025-decoupling-contrastive-deco.tldr: DCD separately learns positive and negative image projections to suppress hallucinations while preserving general reasoning performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Decision trees offer compact, interpretable predictions, but their hard branching decisions make whole-tree gradient optimization difficult. This paper develops an oblique decision tree that can be trained through gradient-based optimization while retaining a unique decision path. The central step is an exact reformulation of hard-split trees using ReLU operations followed by Argmin.

ReLU represents branching constraints through values that are either exactly zero or nonzero. Argmin then selects the unique path with no violations, producing a deterministic prediction. To make training practical, the authors approximate Argmin using a scaled softmin function. A warm-start annealing procedure solves successive optimization problems with increasingly accurate approximations, addressing numerical instability as training moves toward the hard selection behavior.

The reformulation and distributed GPU parallelism support trees of depth twelve on million-scale datasets where most compared baselines fail. Across the reported experiments, the optimized tree exceeds fourteen baselines in test accuracy, including an average improvement of 7.54% over CART. The approach therefore combines joint optimization of the tree with the deterministic routing that makes hard-split trees distinctive.
neurips-2025-differentiable-decision-tre.tldr: A ReLU-and-Argmin reformulation enables gradient-based whole-tree training while retaining deterministic routing and improving reported test accuracy.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models build images through many generation steps, making it difficult to see when particular visual decisions emerge. This paper applies sparse autoencoders to the internal activations of a popular diffusion model. The aim is to identify human-interpretable concepts and follow their spatial arrangement as the image takes shape.

The authors find that activated concepts already reveal substantial information about the final scene composition before the first reverse diffusion step finishes. This is a prediction about the eventual image from very early internal activity. It suggests that meaningful spatial organization becomes visible inside the studied model much earlier than a finished image would.

The paper also intervenes on these representations to test whether they can change generation. Early interventions effectively control composition. By the middle stages, composition is finalized, while style remains responsive to intervention. Near the end, changes are restricted to small textural details. These experiments go beyond observing correlations: they demonstrate different opportunities for control at different stages of the studied model’s generation process.
neurips-2025-emergence-and-evolution-of-.tldr: Sparse autoencoders reveal early scene organization in a diffusion model and enable stage-dependent interventions on composition, style, and texture.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn across a sequence of tasks while making useful connections between them. Knowledge from earlier tasks can help later ones, and later learning can also benefit earlier tasks. This paper argues that methods focused on constraining model updates or dividing parameters can overlook useful information in the relationships between tasks themselves.

The authors introduce H-embedding, a compact representation of a task derived from an information-theoretic measure of transferability. It is designed to be easy to compute online. A hypernetwork uses these representations to generate task-conditioned model weights, allowing information about task relationships to guide the parameters used for each task.

The framework supports end-to-end training and requires storing only a low-dimensional embedding for each task. Evaluations on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and DomainNet report strong performance against baseline and state-of-the-art approaches. The findings support representing how tasks can help one another as a practical ingredient in continual learning, connecting compact task storage with a mechanism for using relationships during model construction.
neurips-2025-exploiting-task-relationshi.tldr: H-embedding represents task transferability and guides a hypernetwork to produce task-specific weights for effective continual learning.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models generate data through a process that must be simulated efficiently at inference time. Exact simulation can have unpredictable runtime and redundant function evaluations. Approximate methods such as tau-leaping offer another route, but their first-order accuracy limits how aggressively they can increase step sizes without introducing error.

This paper develops higher-order numerical inference schemes tailored to discrete diffusion. The goal is to take larger steps while reducing approximation error, improving the use of a fixed computational budget. Its theoretical analysis establishes second-order accuracy in KL divergence for the theta-Trapezoidal method, giving a distribution-level characterization of the solver’s approximation behavior.

The authors evaluate the approach on mathematical reasoning, text generation, and image generation at the stated GSM8K, GPT-2, and ImageNet levels. Under equivalent computational constraints, the method produces better samples than existing approaches, with consistent gains across models ranging from 200 million to eight billion parameters. These results make numerical inference design a concrete route to improving discrete diffusion output quality without increasing the comparison’s computational allowance.
neurips-2025-fast-solvers-for-discrete-d.tldr: Higher-order solvers improve discrete diffusion sampling, with a second-order accuracy guarantee and better reported quality at matched computational cost.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent interactions involving groups of nodes, so useful training data must preserve more than pairwise relationships. HyperMixup addresses two difficulties in learning from these structures: scarce labels and noisy interactions. Ordinary augmentation can disturb the connection between node features and the meanings of hyperedges, undermining the group relationships that the model needs to learn.

The framework guides feature mixing with the hypergraph’s structure. It first pairs nodes using both feature similarity and hyperedge similarity. It then mixes information at two levels while incorporating context to preserve hyperedge meaning. Finally, an adaptive topology reconstruction step maintains consistency while introducing controlled diversity into the augmented data.

The theoretical analysis connects the method’s regularization effects to gradient alignment with hyperedge covariance structures and provides robustness guarantees against combined node and hyperedge perturbations. Experiments across multiple hypergraph learning tasks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, especially when labels are limited. The contribution ties augmentation to group-level structural constraints, making additional training variation more compatible with the relationships encoded by the hypergraph.
neurips-2025-hypermixup-hypergraph-augme.tldr: HyperMixup creates structure-guided hypergraph augmentations that preserve group interactions and improve reported performance, particularly with few labels.

paragraphs: Training networks with low-precision parameters creates a gradient-estimation problem. The straight-through estimator allows backpropagation through quantization, providing useful but biased gradients. Zeroth-order methods offer unbiased gradient estimates, yet obtaining them can be expensive. This paper combines the two sources of information to improve the balance between training quality and computational effort.

The proposed method, First-Order-Guided Zeroth-Order Gradient Descent, uses first-order guidance to reduce the computation associated with zeroth-order optimization while reducing straight-through bias. Its empirical focus is quantization-aware pretraining. At the same number of iterations as the straight-through estimator, it improves accuracy by 1–8% for DeiT Tiny/Small and 1–2% for ResNet 18/50.

For LLaMA models up to 0.3 billion parameters, the reported improvement is 1–22 perplexity points. In a separate comparison on a two-layer MNIST network, reaching the same loss requires 796 times less computation than n-SPSA. These are distinct comparisons: one measures gains at matched iteration counts, while the other measures computation needed for matched loss. Together they support the proposed quality-versus-training-time tradeoff.
neurips-2025-improving-the-straight-thro.tldr: FOGZO combines straight-through and zeroth-order gradient information to improve quantized-network training quality and reduce computation relative to zeroth-order methods.

paragraphs: IPAD tackles the difficulty of distinguishing fluent model-generated text from human writing. The paper focuses on two weaknesses of existing detectors: reduced robustness when data differs from the training distribution or has been attacked, and limited evidence that people can inspect to understand a detection decision.

The framework begins with a Prompt Inverter that predicts prompts capable of producing the input text. Two Distinguishers then examine how likely the text is to align with those predicted prompts. This makes the inferred relationship between a possible instruction and its response part of the detection process, providing material that users can examine alongside the resulting decision.

Against the strongest reported baselines, IPAD improves average recall by 9.05% on in-distribution data and AUROC by 12.93% on out-of-distribution data and 5.48% on attacked data. It also performs robustly on structured datasets. An interpretability assessment supports the value of exposing decision evidence. The reported contribution therefore combines stronger empirical detection with a mechanism for making the basis of a classification more inspectable.
neurips-2025-ipad-inverse-prompt-for-ai-.tldr: IPAD detects generated text by reconstructing plausible prompts and evaluating text–prompt alignment, improving reported robustness while exposing decision evidence.

paragraphs: Giving a language model more computation at inference time raises a practical allocation question. A system can extend a single reasoning sequence, or generate several shorter sequences and combine their answers through a method such as majority voting. Both spend additional computation, but they organize that computation differently.

This paper proves that there are reasoning settings where the sequential option has an exponential advantage over the parallel option. The construction uses graph connectivity problems drawn from challenging graph distributions. The result establishes the existence of a substantial separation: for these settings, many short attempts cannot efficiently substitute for allowing a longer reasoning process.

The authors test the theoretical findings across models trained from scratch for graph connectivity using different reasoning strategies, as well as large reasoning models. These experiments validate the stated theoretical picture. The scope matters: the paper identifies settings favoring sequential scaling, rather than establishing that longer reasoning is always the best allocation. Its contribution is to show that the structure of a reasoning problem can fundamentally affect how additional inference computation should be organized.
neurips-2025-let-me-think-a-long-chain-o.tldr: The paper proves and experimentally supports an exponential advantage for longer sequential reasoning over many short attempts in certain graph-connectivity settings.

paragraphs: Feature visualization interprets a neural network by synthesizing inputs that strongly activate a chosen feature. The resulting image is often treated as evidence of what that feature represents. This paper examines whether that evidence can be deliberately manipulated while leaving the network’s architecture unchanged and avoiding a significant decline in task performance.

Gradient Slingshots alters the optimization trajectories used to produce a visualization. It shapes parts of the feature’s activation landscape outside the data distribution, directing the optimization process toward a predefined target. This exploits the path taken by the visualization procedure, allowing its output to be controlled without requiring a corresponding large change in ordinary predictive performance.

Across several neural network architectures, the authors demonstrate replacement of faithful visualizations with arbitrary target images. The finding exposes a vulnerability for auditors who rely exclusively on this interpretation technique: a convincing visualization may be fabricated. The paper also proposes a straightforward defense and quantitatively demonstrates its effectiveness, showing both a way to manipulate the explanation process and an evaluated response to that manipulation.
neurips-2025-manipulating-feature-visual.tldr: Gradient Slingshots steers feature visualization toward arbitrary images without changing network architecture or significantly degrading performance, exposing an interpretability vulnerability.

paragraphs: Understanding and controlling a language model depends partly on locating internal representations of particular concepts. Sparse autoencoders can extract features from model activations, but those features do not always isolate concepts reliably. This paper addresses monosemanticity: the extent to which a feature has a clear, specific meaning instead of mixing several meanings together.

The authors introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score to quantify that property in latent representations. They then propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders, which condition representations on labeled concepts during training. The method uses explicit concept information to help locate and separate target representations, connecting measurement of feature clarity with a training procedure intended to improve it.

Evaluations cover toxicity detection, writing-style identification, and privacy-attribute recognition. In these settings, the guided approach improves monosemanticity and supports more effective, finer-grained steering with less degradation in output quality. The results link better concept isolation to practical gains in recognizing and influencing model behavior. The work therefore offers both a measurement tool and a supervised way to make extracted representations more useful for interpretation and control.
neurips-2025-measuring-and-guiding-monos.tldr: The paper introduces a monosemanticity metric and concept-guided sparse autoencoders that improve feature isolation and fine-grained model steering.

paragraphs: Link prediction uses information about a pair of nodes to estimate whether they should be connected. Shared neighbors, including higher-order variants, are useful signals for this task. The paper examines why using information from more neighborhood orders does not automatically deliver its full potential: different orders can repeat information and become overly smoothed.

Orthogonal Common Neighbor addresses these problems with two operations. Orthogonalization removes redundancy between common-neighbor features from different orders. Normalization mitigates over-smoothing, helping retain distinctions that would otherwise become less useful. Together, the operations aim to make higher-order relational information contribute more effectively to the final link prediction.

On popular link-prediction benchmarks, OCN exceeds the strongest compared baselines by a reported average of 7.7%. The paper supplies theoretical analysis and ablation studies that support the method and verify the contributions of both operations. Its central insight is that the organization of neighborhood information matters alongside its availability. Separating repeated signals and controlling smoothing can improve the value of features that existing predictors already recognize as important.
neurips-2025-ocn-effectively-utilizing-h.tldr: OCN removes redundancy and mitigates over-smoothing in higher-order common-neighbor features, improving reported link-prediction performance by an average of 7.7%.

paragraphs: An online mixture of experts must decide how to combine a committee’s outputs as new contexts and feedback arrive. This paper frames that problem as expert-guided bandit learning, with aggregate accuracy as the objective. The challenge is to learn which expert combinations or voting patterns are useful while making decisions during the learning process.

The authors propose two algorithms. One combines aggregate voting with an upper-confidence-bound approach to successive elimination, pruning exploration actions that appear suboptimal. The other maintains an online weighted majority vote, assigning each expert voting power in proportion to its predictive power. These approaches offer different mechanisms for adapting the collective decision to observed expert performance.

The paper derives regret guarantees in the bandit setting under ideal circumstances and provides empirical results. It also applies the methods to online fine-tuning with expert language models, dynamically changing expert weights or selecting a committee after responses. The no-regret results are conditional theoretical guarantees, while the application demonstrates how adaptive aggregation can be used to improve the overall performance of a collective model.
neurips-2025-online-mixture-of-experts-n.tldr: Two online expert-aggregation algorithms adapt committee selection or voting weights, with conditional no-regret guarantees and applications to expert language models.

paragraphs: Routing and scheduling with multiple agents require both difficult combinatorial choices and coordination between decision-makers. Learning-based methods can struggle to coordinate agents, generalize to other instances, or produce solutions quickly. PARCO is a reinforcement learning framework designed to construct high-quality multi-agent solutions efficiently by allowing agents to make decisions in parallel.

Three components support this design. Transformer-based communication layers let agents exchange information while building solutions. A multiple pointer mechanism enables parallel choices with low latency. When those choices conflict, a priority-based handler resolves the conflict using learned priorities. These components connect simultaneous decision-making with explicit mechanisms for communication and conflict resolution.

The authors evaluate PARCO on multi-agent vehicle routing and scheduling problems. In those evaluations, it outperforms state-of-the-art learning methods and shows strong generalization and computational efficiency. The approach matters because parallel construction needs coordination to yield useful collective solutions. PARCO places that coordination inside the learned solution-building process, addressing both the quality of the resulting decisions and the time required to produce them.
neurips-2025-parco-parallel-autoregressi.tldr: PARCO combines parallel agent decisions, learned communication, and conflict resolution to improve routing and scheduling performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how additional inference computation can systematically reduce a language model’s chance of producing an incorrect answer. Both proposed algorithms first generate candidate solutions and then use the model to compare them. A minimal implementation needs only black-box access to the model, without a separate verifier or reward model.

The first algorithm selects a winner through a knockout tournament. Its guarantee assumes that the model has a nonzero chance of generating a correct solution and is better than random when comparing a correct solution with an incorrect one. Under those assumptions, failure probability approaches zero exponentially or according to a power law, depending on how computation is increased.

The second algorithm uses a league structure, scoring each candidate by its average win rate against multiple opponents. Under analogous but more robust assumptions, its failure probability decreases exponentially with additional computation. Experiments across multiple models and datasets support the predicted scaling behavior. The contribution provides conditional guarantees for turning generation and comparison into increasingly reliable answers, together with simple procedures for implementing that allocation of compute.
neurips-2025-provable-scaling-laws-for-t.tldr: Knockout and league-style candidate selection provide provable reductions in failure probability as inference compute grows, under stated generation and comparison assumptions.

paragraphs: Online reinforcement learning from human feedback repeatedly collects preferences and refines a model, helping address the limited coverage of a fixed feedback dataset. However, repeatedly accumulating past observations and refitting a reward model creates growing storage and computation costs. This paper targets that reward-modeling bottleneck with updates that process feedback in one pass.

The authors formulate RLHF as a contextual preference bandit and replace standard maximum-likelihood reward modeling with an online mirror descent algorithm using a tailored local norm. The resulting reward-modeling procedure does not need to retain historical data and has constant-time updates per iteration. This makes its update cost independent of the growing number of earlier iterations.

The framework covers passive feedback collection, active collection, and adaptation during deployment. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for improved statistical and computational efficiency, then develop practical algorithms for language models. Experiments with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on Ultrafeedback and Mixture2 validate the approach. The contribution connects an incremental reward-modeling algorithm with several ways of collecting and using preferences online.
neurips-2025-provably-efficient-online-r.tldr: One-pass reward modeling enables online RLHF updates without storing historical feedback, with constant per-iteration update time and theoretical efficiency guarantees.

paragraphs: Autoregressive video generators produce new frames using earlier frames as context. Training on real preceding frames creates a mismatch: during deployment, the context consists of the model’s own imperfect outputs. Self Forcing addresses this exposure bias by having the model generate its own preceding frames during training, bringing the training situation closer to actual generation.

The method performs autoregressive rollouts with key-value caching and evaluates the resulting video through a loss applied to the sequence as a whole. This allows supervision to account for the quality of the generated video beyond individual frames. A few-step diffusion model and stochastic gradient truncation keep the training procedure computationally manageable.

The authors also introduce a rolling key-value cache for efficient video extrapolation. Their experiments demonstrate real-time streaming generation with latency below one second on a single GPU. Generation quality matches or exceeds that of significantly slower non-causal diffusion models in the reported comparisons. The findings support training directly on self-generated context as a way to combine efficient sequential generation with strong overall video quality.
neurips-2025-self-forcing-bridging-the-t.tldr: Self Forcing trains video diffusion models on their own generated context, enabling high-quality real-time streaming with sub-second latency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether explicit reasoning text helps multimodal models during rule-based reinforcement fine-tuning. It first shows that Thinking-RFT improves image classification over supervised fine-tuning and supports cross-dataset generalization. It then introduces No-Thinking-RFT, which uses a simple reward based on answer correctness, to examine whether producing reasoning is responsible for the gains.

Across six tasks and different model sizes and types, No-Thinking-RFT matches or exceeds Thinking-RFT on the evaluated visual perception tasks. Models with limited capabilities struggle to produce useful reasoning chains. Some Thinking-RFT responses also contain inconsistent answers in reasoning and answer sections, and these responses have lower average accuracy. The analysis attributes no-thinking gains to both improved learning and avoiding inference overthinking.

The authors hypothesize that reasoning before a verifiable answer can hinder reward convergence in some settings, and test placing reasoning after the answer. A pilot Adaptive-Thinking method learns to think or refrain depending on model capability, reaching comparable or better performance than either fixed strategy. The findings suggest that explicit reasoning should depend on capabilities and task complexity.
neurips-2025-to-think-or-not-to-think-a-.tldr: Explicit reasoning does not consistently help visual reinforcement fine-tuning, and a pilot adaptive method learns whether to use it.

paragraphs: Understanding a long video can require connecting two brief events separated by substantial intervening material. Causal2Needles evaluates whether video-language models can find those events and jointly interpret cause and effect in human behavior. The benchmark targets a combination of information retrieval and causal understanding that the authors consider insufficiently tested by existing evaluations.

Its questions distinguish noncausal single-event retrieval, causal single-event understanding, and causal reasoning involving two events. The hardest category requires information about both cause and effect from the video and associated narration. To prevent textual bias, the benchmark uses complementary answer formats: identifying the relevant video clip and describing a visual detail within that clip.

Experiments show that models performing well on existing benchmarks struggle with causal two-event questions. Performance is negatively correlated with the distance between the two relevant events, linking greater separation with greater difficulty. These findings expose weaknesses in connecting distributed evidence across a long video. They also explain why strong results on other benchmarks may leave this particular combination of retrieval and causal interpretation inadequately assessed.
neurips-2025-two-causally-related-needle.tldr: Causal2Needles reveals that strong video-language models struggle to connect causally related events, with performance worsening as those events become farther apart.

paragraphs: Prompting adapts a pretrained model through its input, but the reasons it succeeds or fails are often studied empirically. This paper develops a Bayesian account through meta-learning. It explains how meta-trained networks behave as predictors over their pretraining distribution, with rapid adaptation to information in context as a characteristic feature.

Within this account, choosing an optimal prompt becomes a conditioning problem for a Bayesian predictor. That formulation yields criteria for target tasks where optimal prompting is possible and where it is not. It also identifies fundamental prompting limits that require weight tuning to overcome. Educational experiments with LSTMs and Transformers compare prefix-tuning variants with methods that modify network weights.

The paper additionally examines soft prefixes: real-valued input vectors that need not correspond to ordinary tokens. These can produce effective prompts for trained and even untrained networks by changing activations in ways discrete tokens cannot achieve. This finding adds a mechanistic perspective alongside the Bayesian account, showing that prompt effectiveness can also depend on the kinds of internal manipulation the input representation permits.
neurips-2025-understanding-prompt-tuning.tldr: A Bayesian meta-learning view explains when prompting can work, while soft-prefix experiments reveal additional mechanisms for manipulating network activations.
